subject: environmental-science
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A groundwater aquifer that recharges only slowly, and fish stocks that can regrow if not over-harvested, are both examples of:
options: Perpetual resources
Natural capital with no income value
Replenishable (renewable but depletable) resources
Non-renewable resources
questions.explain: Replenishable resources renew naturally but can be exhausted if exploited faster than their rate of replacement.

questions.q: An age-sex pyramid with a very wide base that narrows steeply toward the top most directly indicates a population with:
options: A declining population with negative natural increase
A high birth rate and rapid growth
A high proportion of elderly and low fertility
Zero population growth and an even age structure
questions.explain: A wide base reflects many young people and a high birth rate, the signature of a rapidly growing population.

questions.q: 'Dematerialisation' as a strategy to reduce environmental impact means:
options: Banning the manufacture of new products
Delivering the same service or value using less material and energy
Replacing all goods with digital alternatives only
Moving production offshore to other countries
questions.explain: Dematerialisation reduces the quantity of materials and energy embodied in a product or service while maintaining its function.

questions.q: The crude death rate is calculated as:
options: Deaths per 1,000 live births per year
The percentage of the population that is elderly
Deaths per 1,000 people in the population per year
Deaths minus births per year
questions.explain: The crude death rate expresses the number of deaths per 1,000 individuals in the total population over a year.

questions.q: Under the 'demographic dividend', a country can experience accelerated economic growth when:
options: A large share of the population is of working age relative to dependants
The dependency ratio rises sharply with many elderly
Birth rates and death rates are both very high
Net migration becomes strongly negative
questions.explain: As fertility falls, the working-age share grows relative to young and old dependants, freeing resources for investment and raising output per capita.

questions.q: Composting of biodegradable household waste is best described within the waste hierarchy as a form of:
options: Source reduction
Disposal
Recovery / recycling of organic matter
Energy generation by incineration
questions.explain: Composting recovers nutrients from organic waste and returns them to soils, diverting biodegradable material from landfill.

questions.q: A population grows at a constant rate of 2% per year. Approximately how long is its doubling time, using the 'rule of 70'?
options: 140 years
35 years
14 years
70 years
questions.explain: Doubling time is roughly 70 divided by the annual percentage growth rate, so 70 / 2 = 35 years.

questions.q: The Montreal Protocol (1987) is widely regarded as a successful international environmental agreement because it:
options: Banned commercial whaling worldwide
Phased out the production of ozone-depleting substances such as CFCs
Set binding national limits on carbon dioxide emissions
Created a global market for trading biodiversity credits
questions.explain: The Montreal Protocol committed nations to eliminating CFCs and other ozone-depleting substances, leading to measurable recovery of the stratospheric ozone layer.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a circular economy?
options: Products and materials are kept in use through reuse, repair and recycling so waste is minimised
Economic growth is decoupled entirely from any resource use
Resources flow linearly from extraction to disposal as quickly as possible
Waste is exported to other countries to keep domestic landfills empty
questions.explain: A circular economy designs out waste by cycling materials back into production through reuse, remanufacture and recycling, contrasting with the linear 'take-make-dispose' model.

questions.q: Incineration of municipal solid waste with energy recovery is sometimes preferred over landfill primarily because it:
options: Greatly reduces waste volume and can generate electricity or heat
Produces no atmospheric emissions whatsoever
Eliminates the need for any pollution control equipment
Recovers all materials for direct reuse
questions.explain: Incineration can reduce waste volume by around 90% and recover energy, though it still requires flue-gas cleaning to limit dioxins and particulates.

questions.q: Recycling aluminium rather than smelting it from bauxite ore is environmentally advantageous mainly because it:
options: Uses roughly 95% less energy than primary production
Generates more solid waste
Eliminates the need for any collection system
Produces a stronger metal
questions.explain: Recycling aluminium requires only about 5% of the energy needed to extract and refine it from ore, greatly cutting emissions.

questions.q: In environmental economics, 'natural capital' refers to:
options: The money governments invest in renewable energy
The cost of cleaning up after an environmental disaster
The financial value of land owned by conservation charities
The stock of natural resources and ecosystems that yield a flow of goods and services
questions.explain: Natural capital is the stock of natural assets (forests, soils, fisheries, the atmosphere) that provides ongoing 'natural income' of goods and ecosystem services.

questions.q: In the waste hierarchy, which sequence correctly ranks the options from MOST to LEAST preferred?
options: Dispose > recover > recycle > reuse > reduce
Reuse > reduce > dispose > recover > recycle
Reduce > reuse > recycle > recover > dispose
Recycle > reuse > reduce > recover > dispose
questions.explain: The waste hierarchy prioritises prevention first: reduce, then reuse, then recycle, then recover (e.g. energy), with disposal as the last resort.

questions.q: The principle of 'intergenerational equity' in sustainable development requires that:
options: All resources are converted to financial capital
Only the wealthiest nations conserve resources
The current generation maximises resource use now
Future generations inherit a stock of natural capital comparable to today's
questions.explain: Intergenerational equity holds that present use of resources should not compromise the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

questions.q: The 'tragedy of the commons' explains environmental degradation by arguing that:
options: Government ownership guarantees sustainable use
Individuals acting in self-interest can overexploit a shared, open-access resource
Privately owned resources are always overexploited
Resources with a market price are never depleted
questions.explain: When a resource is open-access and unregulated, each user gains the full benefit of exploiting it while the costs are shared, driving collective overuse.

questions.q: Which factor would most likely RAISE the total fertility rate in a population?
options: Rising urbanisation and the cost of raising children
Improved availability of contraception
Increased female education and workforce participation
High infant mortality and the use of children as agricultural labour
questions.explain: High infant mortality encourages couples to have more children, and the economic value of child labour in subsistence economies further raises fertility.

questions.q: In the Demographic Transition Model (DTM), Stage 2 is characterised by which combination of vital rates?
options: High birth rates and rapidly falling death rates
Falling birth rates and low death rates
Low birth rates and low death rates
High death rates and high birth rates that fluctuate
questions.explain: DTM Stage 2 shows persistently high birth rates while death rates fall sharply (due to improved sanitation, food and medicine), producing rapid population growth.

questions.q: A key environmental drawback of disposing of solid domestic waste in landfill, compared with other methods, is the release of:
options: Chlorofluorocarbons from refrigerant breakdown
Sulfur dioxide from combustion
Ozone from photochemical reactions
Methane, a potent greenhouse gas, from anaerobic decomposition
questions.explain: Organic waste decomposing anaerobically in landfill generates methane, which has a far higher global warming potential than CO2 over a century.

questions.q: Natural increase rate of a population is best calculated as:
options: Birth rate plus immigration
Death rate minus emigration
Birth rate minus death rate
Fertility rate divided by mortality rate
questions.explain: Natural increase (excluding migration) equals the crude birth rate minus the crude death rate.

questions.q: According to the IPAT model, a technological improvement that halves the resource impact per unit of consumption, with population and affluence unchanged, would:
options: Halve the total environmental impact
Leave total impact unchanged
Double the total environmental impact
Eliminate environmental impact entirely
questions.explain: Because impact is the product of the three terms, halving the technology factor halves total impact when the other factors are constant.

questions.q: In Stage 4 of the Demographic Transition Model, the population typically:
options: Declines because death rates exceed birth rates
Grows explosively due to falling death rates
Is stable or grows slowly with low birth and low death rates
Fluctuates with high birth and high death rates
questions.explain: Stage 4 features both low birth and low death rates, giving a large but stable or only slowly growing population.

questions.q: A factory discharges waste into a river, imposing clean-up and health costs on downstream communities that are not reflected in the factory's prices. This is an example of:
options: A positive externality
A market subsidy
An internalised cost
A negative externality
questions.explain: A negative externality is a cost of an activity borne by third parties rather than by the producer or consumer, so the market price understates the true social cost.

questions.q: Imposing a tax on each tonne of carbon emitted is intended to correct a market failure by:
options: Internalising the external cost so the polluter pays
Increasing the externality so consumers pay less
Removing the need for any regulation
Subsidising fossil-fuel extraction
questions.explain: A carbon (Pigouvian) tax forces emitters to bear the social cost of pollution, aligning private cost with social cost under the 'polluter pays' principle.

questions.q: In the IPAT model, environmental impact (I) is expressed as the product of:
options: Inputs, processes and throughputs
Population, affluence and technology
Industry, agriculture and trade
Income, pollution and technology
questions.explain: IPAT states Impact = Population x Affluence (consumption per person) x Technology (impact per unit of consumption).

questions.q: In environmental systems terminology, a resource such as solar energy that is continuously available regardless of how much is used is best classified as:
options: A non-renewable resource
A replenishable resource
A renewable (perpetual) resource
A recyclable resource
questions.explain: Renewable/perpetual resources like solar, wind and tidal energy are effectively inexhaustible on human timescales irrespective of consumption.

questions.q: Which of the following best illustrates 'reuse' rather than 'recycling' in the waste hierarchy?
options: Melting glass bottles to make new glass
Composting food scraps
Refilling and re-selling the same glass milk bottles
Burning waste to generate electricity
questions.explain: Reuse keeps a product in its existing form for the same or a new purpose, whereas recycling reprocesses materials into new products.

questions.q: A 'cap-and-trade' (emissions trading) scheme reduces pollution by:
options: Setting an overall emissions cap and allowing firms to buy and sell allowances
Subsidising the most polluting industries
Banning all emissions immediately
Removing any limit on total emissions
questions.explain: A cap fixes the total quantity of emissions, and tradable permits let reductions occur where they are cheapest, using the market to achieve the target efficiently.

questions.q: The 'replacement fertility' level for a developed country is usually quoted as a total fertility rate (TFR) of about:
questions.explain: A TFR of roughly 2.1 children per woman replaces both parents while allowing for childhood mortality, so the population stabilises long-term.

questions.q: A 'sustainable yield' for a renewable resource such as a forest is the:
options: Maximum amount that can be harvested in a single year regardless of regrowth
Amount left after all economically valuable timber is removed
Total standing stock of the resource
Rate of harvest that does not exceed the resource's rate of natural replenishment
questions.explain: Sustainable yield is the harvest rate that equals natural replacement, allowing indefinite use without depleting the resource base.

questions.q: A cost-benefit analysis (CBA) of a proposed wetland drainage scheme would conclude the project is economically justified only if:
options: Public opposition is below 50%
No species are lost
The total benefits to the developer exceed zero
The discounted social benefits exceed the discounted social costs
questions.explain: CBA recommends a project when the present value of all social benefits exceeds the present value of all social costs, including environmental externalities.
